name: Kira Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Kira, thanks for talking to me. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a designer at Loudspeaker, a five-person studio that makes campaign graphics for charities, tenant groups and a couple of climate organisations. Most days it's social ads, short animated clips and the odd logo, all on deadline because campaigns move fast. I use AI tools every single day, for rough storyboards, quick background images, captions and resizing, and then I do the real design on top. I love the speed; what wears me out is when a campaign changes its whole message at eleven at night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how are things money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with two friends near the market, no partner at the moment. I've got about two months of expenses saved, which is fine but not much if something went wrong. Pay is normal for a studio designer, so I'm not struggling, but I'm not getting ahead either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly. I'd post something like, turns out the robots are just very fast interns. At work I'd tell the team we keep using the tools for the boring bits and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's probably the best outcome for me. I already use the tools more than anyone at Loudspeaker, so I'd stay the quick one, and nobody's job really vanishes. The thing I'd still watch is charity funding, because when grants dry up our clients cut the design budget first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and push to teach the others the tools I use so the whole studio gets faster. I'd try to grow my savings from two months to four, because campaign work comes in waves. Maybe I'd pick up some evening freelance doing animated explainers for small unions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little flat, because I find the change exciting, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said grants drying up is the real risk. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year one climate group lost a big donor and we lost about a third of a month's work overnight. Our director Femi shuffled everyone onto other clients, but it was tight. So yes, money worries exist with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would teaching the others the tools change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me useful in a way that isn't just making ads. If I'm the one who knows how to get the best out of the tools, I'm harder to let go. And it's nicer when the whole team is fast, not just me.

say: I'd joke that the robots are just **very fast interns**.
I'd tell the team to keep using the tools for the **boring bits**.
think: Plateau is probably the **best outcome** for me, since I'm already the quickest with the tools.
The real risk is **charity funding**, because clients cut design first when grants dry up.
do: Teach my **colleagues** the tools I use so the studio gets faster.
Grow savings from **two months to four**, since campaign work comes in waves.
Pick up **evening freelance** making explainers for small unions.
feel: **Fine**, if a little **flat**, because I find the change exciting.
S0.quote: Turns out the robots are just very fast interns.
fieldNote: She is **eager** for change and slightly disappointed when it doesn't come.
Her real exposure is **grant-funded clients**, which she has already felt once.
Being the studio's **tool teacher** is her strategy to stay valuable.

steps.text: Run short sessions teaching her colleagues the AI tools
Save toward four months of expenses
Take evening freelance making animated explainers for small unions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the gains don't all go to the people at the top. I'd be posting about shorter weeks, not fewer jobs. At work I'd say let's use this to take on more campaigns, not cut people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the people who comes out okay. I already work the way the card describes, with AI doing the first draft and me doing the judgement. The ones I'd worry about are designers like my old uni friends who refuse to touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a proper course in AI video and motion tools this year, paid out of my own pocket if Femi won't cover it. I'd pitch a new service to our clients, campaign videos made in a day instead of a week. And I'd push for the studio to become a worker co-op, so if it gets more profitable, we all share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a small worry in the back. I don't love that my friends are scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd come out okay. What if Femi decides one Kira can do the work of three designers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me honest. If that happened I'd be the one left, and I'd feel terrible about it. That's partly why I want a co-op, so it's not just Femi's decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the friends who won't touch the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I get it, the tools were trained on our work without asking, and that's a real fight. But I'd also say this: refusing the tools doesn't stop AI, it just stops you having a say. I'd offer to sit with them for an evening.

say: I'd say the **gains** mustn't all go to the people at the top.
I'd post about **shorter weeks**, not fewer jobs.
think: I already work **AI-first** with my judgement on top, so I probably come out okay.
I'd worry about **friends** who refuse to touch the tools.
do: Take a course in **AI video tools** this year, paid myself if needed.
Pitch **one-day campaign videos** to our existing clients.
Push for the studio to become a **worker co-op**.
feel: **Excited**, with a small worry about **scared friends**.
S1.quote: Refusing the tools doesn't stop AI, it just stops you having a say.
fieldNote: She sees herself as a **likely winner** and feels guilty about it.
Her progressive views show up as a push for a **worker co-op**, not just protest.
Her own job looks safe, so the mood is **uneasy** rather than calm.

steps.text: Take an evening course in AI video and motion tools
Pitch one-day campaign videos to Loudspeaker's clients
Propose turning Loudspeaker into a worker co-op

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who said it was hype were wrong, and now we need a plan for everyone. I'd be campaigning for a public stake in the AI companies, because if they do all the work, the money has to come back to people. I'd use my skills to make the campaign graphics, obviously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one gets me too. If AI can do any thinking work as well as me, then knowing the tools stops being special within a year. My job is almost all screen work, so there's no three-year cushion for me like there is for a plumber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd save hard, aim for six months, and stop paying for nice things. I'd throw myself into organising, because campaign groups will need people who can run AI well in a crisis, and maybe that's paid work for a while. Once it lands, I'd look at getting into something human, like community organising itself, where people want a person to show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy. I've always liked being ahead, and this is the first one where being ahead doesn't help much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots matter to you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for my design job, no. It matters for my flatmates, one's a chef and one's a carpenter, so they'd outlast me. I might end up being the one who needs help with the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second streaming service, the takeaways, and the trip to see my cousins in the summer. That last one would hurt. But two months of savings isn't much when your whole field changes in two years.

say: I'd campaign for a **public stake** in the AI companies.
I'd say we need **a plan for everyone**, not just the people who saw it coming.
think: Knowing the tools **stops being special** within a year.
My job is almost all screen work, so there's **no three-year cushion** for me.
do: Save hard toward **six months** and cut takeaways and subscriptions.
Do **paid organising work** helping campaign groups use AI in a crisis.
Look at **community organising** as a long-term job where a person must show up.
feel: **Dizzy**, because being ahead **doesn't help much** this time.
S2.quote: My job is almost all screen work, so there's no three-year cushion for me like there is for a plumber.
fieldNote: Even the most **adaptive** designer expects to lose her job here, and she says so.
She notices her **flatmates' hands-on jobs** outlast hers, flipping who might need help.
Her answer is **political and practical**: public stake, organising work, savings.

steps.text: Cut takeaways, a streaming service and the summer trip
Save toward six months of expenses
Take paid work helping campaign groups run AI tools
Campaign for a public stake in AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we can't waste. I'd push the groups I work with to put AI and work at the top of their campaigns. I'd also say to other designers, start now, don't wait for 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get three or four good years out of design, maybe more because I'm quick with the tools. After that I need to be doing something where people want a human. I'd be thirty-two, which is a good age to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep designing and use every tool, and I'd save harder, aiming for six months by 2029. I'd start a part-time course in community organising or mediation, something with people. And I'd keep pushing the co-op idea at Loudspeaker so we can steer the change together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but focused. I'd have a plan and a deadline, which I actually work well with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mediation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've sat in a lot of tenant meetings. Someone calm in a room full of shouting tenants changes everything, and I can't see an AI doing that in a way people trust. I might be wrong, but it's where I'd bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do any of this alone, or with others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With others, definitely. I'd want a few designers from different studios meeting once a month to share what's working. That's how I learned half my tools anyway.

I'd tell other designers to **start now**, not in 2030.
think: I get **three or four** good years of design before it ends.

do: Take a part-time course in **mediation or organising**.
Start a monthly **designers' meetup** across studios.
feel: **Nervous but focused**, because a deadline helps me work.
S3.quote: Someone calm in a room full of shouting tenants changes everything, and I can't see an AI doing that in a way people trust.
fieldNote: More time lets her **plan a pivot** toward work built on trust.
She draws the idea from **tenant meetings**, a concrete part of her client work.
She thinks **collectively**, setting up a cross-studio group rather than going alone.

steps.text: Save toward six months of expenses by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to get this right, if we actually use it. I'd push for a law that ties AI profits to retraining money. I'd also tell people not to panic, because panic makes for bad choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is most of my design career anyway. I'd be thirty-seven, and I'd probably have moved into something else by then for other reasons. So it doesn't scare me much for myself, it scares me for people with kids and mortgages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Loudspeaker and keep learning every tool as it comes. I'd build my freelance work into a small side business making campaign videos. In maybe five years, I'd start training in mediation or organising so I'm ready before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit restless. It's far enough off that I'd keep forgetting, then remembering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it scares you for people with kids. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Femi, our director, who has two kids and a mortgage and the whole studio on his shoulders. He'd have to decide who stays. I wouldn't want to be him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year version that you'd actually look forward to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shorter weeks, if we fight for them. If AI does the dull parts, I'd love a four-day week and time to do my own art. That only happens if workers push for it.

I'd push for a law tying **AI profits** to retraining money.

It scares me more for **people with kids** and mortgages than for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's the one where being good with the tools stops helping. What would help is a public share in what these companies earn, so people like me have something to live on while we change. And somewhere to retrain that doesn't cost a year's wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who's in the room when these decisions get made. Right now it's the companies and a few governments. Designers, carers, cleaners, none of us are in the room when these decisions get made, and we should be.

headlineQuote: Designers, carers, cleaners, none of us are in the room when these decisions get made, and we should be.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old designer** at a five-person studio making campaign graphics for charities and tenant groups.
She uses AI tools **daily**, shares a flat with two friends and has about **two months** saved.
She sees herself as a winner in slow change, but expects to **lose design work** when AGI comes fast.
Her plans mix **savings, organising** and a move toward mediation or community work.
Her politics are hands-on: a **worker co-op**, a public stake in AI firms and shorter weeks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because being good with the tools stops helping.
